Many reads: cache. Many writes: queues and partitioning

items.text: "Slow" is worse than "down". A slow part holds its callers until they have no capacity.
Retry at one level only. Three levels of three retries make one failure 27 calls.
Retry only operations that are safe to repeat. Wait longer each time, add a random part, set a maximum.
For each box of which there is only one, add a second or state why you accept the risk.
The limit is usually the database, not the application servers.
Measure percentiles, not averages. An average hides the slow requests.
Do the estimate in the first ten minutes. Write units, and state what the result means.
Test each integration point against a harness that fails on purpose: no answer, slow bytes, wrong formats.
Every wait has a limit. Every resource has an owner and a size.
Use a retry budget of about 10% of traffic. Retry a timeout or a 503, not a 400.
Give each request an ID at the entry point, and pass it to each part.
Select the SLO from what users need. Each added "9" costs much more.
Alert on what users feel. Each alert must need an action from a person now.
"No events" looks like "all is well". Use a signal that must arrive, such as a canary check.
Change the database in steps: add the column, use it, remove the old one later.
Check access for each record, in the service that owns the data.
Fail closed: when a check cannot be made, refuse.
Mark test accounts and orders in production. Exclude them from reports. Never charge a real card.
Make rollback the default first action for a bad release. It needs no diagnosis.
A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Do not put secrets or sensitive personal data in it.

blocks.title: Stability antipatterns
rows: Calls that hang, odd errors from another system
Timeouts, circuit breakers, a test harness
A healthy layer fails after the layer below it fails
Identical servers fail one after another
Bulkheads, fix the leak, spare capacity
Process is up, but throughput is zero
The back end fails when the front end scales out
Pools sized from back-end capacity, back pressure, shed load
Load spikes at deploy, on the hour, or at cache expiry
Random jitter, staggered starts, request coalescing
Automation removes or changes much of the fleet
Memory or response time grows with data age
A limit on every query, pagination

items.text: Stop the bleeding first: roll back, turn off a flag, or move traffic. Find the cause later.
Ask "what changed?". A recent change is the most common cause of an incident.
Declare an incident early: a second team must help, customers see it, or one hour passes.
Keep end-to-end tests to a few core journeys. An end-to-end gate on all services couples their releases.
Keep postmortems blameless. Give each action item an owner, a priority, and a ticket.
Keep toil and other operations work at or below 50% of the team's time.
Measure the four key metrics together: lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, time to restore.
Speed and stability go together. The best teams are better on all four metrics.
An external change approval board did not reduce change failures. Peer review and automated tests worked better.
Services that must deploy together are a distributed monolith, often slower than the monolith they replaced.
